opus-5.5.text:
I think this is actually where architecture design matters the most, and it's a bit different from the large-model world.

For large models trained on huge clusters, the architecture question has converged quite a lot. Transformers are a very general, very hardware-friendly structure, and at that scale the dominant factors are data, compute, and the training recipe. Small tweaks to the architecture often get washed out as you scale up. So in the large-model regime I'd say architecture is important but not the main lever.

When you go down to small models on specific hardware, a phone chip, an NPU, an edge device, things change. Your budget is very tight: latency, memory bandwidth, power, sometimes even which operators the chip supports. In that setting, the gap between a well-designed architecture and a naive one can be huge, not a few percent but sometimes several times in actual speed at the same accuracy.

One lesson we learned back in the ShuffleNet days is that FLOPs is not the right metric. Many people designed networks to minimize FLOPs or parameter counts, but on real hardware the speed was disappointing, because what really dominates is memory access cost, the degree of parallelism, the number of fragmented operations, element-wise ops, and so on. That's why in ShuffleNet V2 we proposed some practical guidelines, like keeping channel widths balanced, avoiding too much group convolution, reducing network fragmentation. The core idea was that you have to design against the real hardware, measure real latency, not a proxy.

I think the same principle holds today for small language models or multimodal models on device. You need to co-design with the hardware. For example, attention's KV cache is a big memory burden on the edge, so the choice between full attention, linear attention, sliding window, or hybrid structures becomes very important. Quantization friendliness matters too. Some architectures are much more robust to low-bit quantization than others, and that directly decides whether you can deploy it at all.

So my judgment is: in the big-model era, architecture is somewhat secondary to scaling. But once you face concrete hardware constraints, architecture becomes first-class again. It's really an engineering optimization problem with many constraints, and good design there gives you returns that more data or more training simply can't.

r001.rationale: The response says architecture is secondary for large models but becomes first-class for small models under tight hardware budgets, where design choices can cause large speed differences.

r002.rationale: It discusses designing and measuring for specific hardware, but does not state that the same model’s runtime efficiency can vary substantially across different devices.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify neural architecture search as a way to automate hardware-specific model design.

fable-5.1.text:
Actually, I think architecture design matters a lot more than most people assume, and the reason is that the trade-offs are completely different once you move away from a cluster of GPUs.

When you train a large model in the cloud, compute is abundant and the only thing you really care about is scaling—more data, more parameters, let the hardware absorb the cost. But when you deploy on a phone, a car, a camera, or a robot, you're suddenly bound by very concrete constraints: memory bandwidth, power budget, latency, the specific operators the NPU actually accelerates. The same FLOPs can run at wildly different speeds depending on whether your network is memory-bound or compute-bound, whether the activation layouts match the chip, whether the operators are fused well. So at that point, the architecture is no longer an abstract question; it's the interface between the algorithm and the physics of the device.

What I learned over the years—going back to ShuffleNet and later RepVGG—is that FLOPs are a very misleading proxy. Two networks with identical FLOPs can differ by two or three times in real latency because of memory access cost, fragmentation of operators, or how parallelizable the structure is. So good small-model architecture design is really about designing for the hardware's actual bottlenecks, not for a number on paper.

The second thing is that small models can't afford waste. A large model has so much redundancy that a mediocre architecture still works—scale hides mistakes. A small model has no such margin. Every parameter has to be doing useful work, so the inductive bias you build into the structure matters much more. That's why, counterintuitively, I think architecture research is more valuable at the small end than at the large end right now.

And there's a third point: you shouldn't think of it as "shrink the big model." Distillation and compression are useful, but the best results usually come from co-designing the architecture with the hardware and the data pipeline from the start—deciding what the model needs to be good at, what the chip is good at, and finding a structure that sits in the intersection. If you just prune a large model, you inherit all its design assumptions, and most of those assumptions were made for a different environment.

So, to answer your question directly: for large models, architecture is maybe secondary to data and scale. For small models on specific hardware, architecture is often the deciding factor between something that works in a demo and something that actually ships.

r002.rationale: It says identical-FLOP networks can differ two or three times in real latency, depending on hardware bottlenecks and operator support.

r003.rationale: It discusses co-designing architectures with hardware and data, but does not identify neural architecture search as an automation method.

astra-6.text:
I think architecture design becomes more important when you move from a large model to a small model deployed on specific hardware. With a large model, you have more room to compensate through scale. With a small model, you have a tighter budget, so how you allocate computation and capacity matters a great deal.

And that budget is not just the number of parameters or FLOPs. What you actually care about is latency, memory consumption, power, and the accuracy you can achieve within those constraints. An operation that looks inexpensive on paper may run poorly on your target device because of memory access or limited operator support. So a model with fewer FLOPs is not necessarily faster.

For me, the key is to make architecture design part of a feedback loop with deployment. You design a candidate, measure it on the actual hardware, and use those measurements to guide the next iteration. Training and compression still matter, of course, but the architecture determines how effectively the model can use the hardware available to it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think architecture design becomes more important as you move toward smaller models deployed on specific hardware. With a large model, you can often improve performance by increasing capacity. With a small model, you have much less room, so you need to think carefully about how to use that capacity and whether the hardware can execute the model efficiently.

The key is that fewer FLOPs or fewer parameters do not necessarily mean lower latency. Different operators can have very different efficiencies on a particular device. Memory access, data movement, and the support provided by the inference framework all affect the result. An architecture that looks efficient on paper may not be efficient in deployment.

So I would treat architecture, training, and deployment as a joint problem. Start with the task and the hardware constraints, measure performance on the actual device, and use those measurements to guide the design. The goal is to get the best accuracy within the latency, memory, and power budget—not simply to make the model smaller.
